_link.title: I can describe the role of stem cells in multicellular organisms

toLevel2.question: What are the two main roles of stem cells in multicellular organisms?

options.text: Producing specialised cells during development and repairing tissue in adult life
options.explanation: Stem cells differentiate to produce specialised cell types during embryonic development and repair/maintain tissues throughout adult life.
Energy production and nutrient storage are functions of specialised cells, not the roles of stem cells.
These are functions of red and white blood cells, which are produced by stem cells, not roles of stem cells themselves.
Digestion and excretion are organ-level functions, not the roles of stem cells.

toLevel2.question: What do embryonic stem cells of the inner cell mass differentiate into?

options.explanation: Embryonic stem cells from the inner cell mass differentiate into ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, which then produce all specialised cell types.
Blood cells are one of many cell types produced; embryonic stem cells give rise to all 210+ specialised cell types.
Nerve cells are just one type; embryonic stem cells produce all cell types through the germ layers.
Muscle cells come from one germ layer; embryonic stem cells produce cells from all three germ layers.

toLevel2.question: How often are skin cells replaced in adults?

options.explanation: Epithelial stem cells in the skin continuously replace skin cells that are lost approximately every 2-4 weeks.
Red blood cells are replaced every 4 months; skin cells are replaced more frequently.
Skin cell replacement is much more frequent than annually.
Skin cells are constantly shed and replaced by stem cell division.

toLevel2.question: Which stem cells replace red blood cells in adults?

options.text: Haematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow
options.explanation: Haematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow produce new red blood cells, replacing them approximately every 4 months.

options.text: Epithelial stem cells in the skin
options.explanation: Epithelial stem cells replace skin cells, not red blood cells.

options.text: Neural stem cells in the brain
options.explanation: Neural stem cells are found in the brain and are not responsible for blood cell production.

options.text: Stem cells in the stomach lining
options.explanation: Stomach lining stem cells replace gut lining cells, not red blood cells.

toLevel2.question: How many specialised cell types are produced from embryonic stem cells in the human body?

options.explanation: Embryonic stem cells differentiate through the three germ layers to produce over 210 specialised cell types in the human body.
The human body has far more than 10 specialised cell types.
Three refers to the number of germ layers, not the total number of specialised cell types.
The actual number is much higher — over 210 specialised cell types.

toLevel2.question: Stem cells only play a role during embryonic development and are not needed in adult life.
toLevel2.explanation: Stem cells play essential roles throughout life. In adults, they continuously repair and maintain tissues, such as replacing skin cells and blood cells.

toLevel2.question: Haematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow replace red blood cells approximately every 4 months.
toLevel2.explanation: Red blood cells have a lifespan of about 4 months, and haematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow continuously produce new ones to replace them.

toLevel2.question: During development, stem cells {{1}} to produce all the specialised cell types needed for a functional {{2}}.
In adults, {{1}} stem cells in the skin replace skin cells every 2-4 weeks.
Stem cells serve two main roles: producing specialised cells during {{1}} and repairing {{2}} in adult life.

toLevel3.question: Why are stem cells essential for both embryonic development and adult tissue maintenance?

options.text: Because they are the source of all new specialised cells, whether for building the body or replacing worn-out cells
options.explanation: Stem cells provide the ongoing supply of new cells needed both during initial body construction (development) and ongoing maintenance (repair).

options.text: Because they produce energy for the body
options.explanation: Energy production is a function of mitochondria, not the primary role of stem cells.
Fighting infections is a function of white blood cells, which are produced by stem cells but is not the stem cells' direct role.

options.text: Because they store genetic information only
options.explanation: All cells store genetic information; stem cells are unique because they can differentiate and self-renew.

toLevel3.question: Explain why the inner cell mass is significant for producing all body cell types.

options.text: Because inner cell mass cells are pluripotent and can differentiate into the three germ layers, which produce all specialised types
options.explanation: The pluripotent inner cell mass cells give rise to ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, from which all 210+ cell types in the body are derived.

options.text: Because inner cell mass cells are already specialised
options.explanation: Inner cell mass cells are unspecialised (pluripotent); their importance lies in their ability to become specialised.
The trophoblast forms the placenta; the inner cell mass forms the embryo.

options.text: Because they only produce blood cells
options.explanation: Inner cell mass cells can produce all body cell types, not just blood cells.

toLevel3.question: Why do different tissues have different rates of stem cell-mediated replacement?

options.text: Because tissues exposed to more wear and damage need faster replacement to maintain function
options.explanation: Skin (2-4 week replacement) is constantly exposed to the environment, while red blood cells (4 month replacement) face less physical wear but have a limited functional lifespan.

options.text: Because all tissues replace cells at the same rate
options.explanation: Different tissues have very different replacement rates based on their exposure and functional needs.
Stem cell division is regulated according to tissue needs, not random.

options.text: Because only skin cells use stem cells for replacement
options.explanation: Many tissues use stem cells for replacement, including bone marrow, gut lining and skin.

toLevel3.question: How does the role of stem cells in development differ from their role in adult repair?

options.text: In development they create new cell types from scratch; in repair they replace existing cell types that have been lost
options.explanation: Developmental stem cells build the organism's cellular diversity, while adult stem cells maintain existing tissue by replacing cells that wear out or are damaged.

options.text: There is no difference; both roles are identical
options.explanation: The roles differ: development involves creating diversity while repair involves maintaining existing tissues.

options.text: Development uses adult stem cells while repair uses embryonic stem cells
options.explanation: Development uses embryonic stem cells; repair primarily uses adult stem cells.

options.text: Stem cells are only active during development
options.explanation: Stem cells remain active throughout life for tissue repair and maintenance.

toLevel3.question: Why is it important that stem cells can both self-renew and differentiate?

options.text: Self-renewal maintains the stem cell pool while differentiation produces needed specialised cells
options.explanation: Without self-renewal, the stem cell population would be depleted. Without differentiation, no new specialised cells would be produced. Both are essential.

options.text: Because only one function is needed at any time
options.explanation: Both functions operate simultaneously to maintain tissues.

options.text: Because self-renewal and differentiation are the same process
options.explanation: They are distinct processes: self-renewal produces more stem cells, differentiation produces specialised cells.

options.text: Because only self-renewal matters for organism survival
options.explanation: Both are essential; without differentiation, specialised cells needed for tissue function would not be produced.

toLevel3.question: Explain the connection between stem cell activity and the concept that all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

options.text: Stem cells are the pre-existing cells that divide to produce both new stem cells and new specialised cells
options.explanation: The principle that all cells come from pre-existing cells is directly demonstrated by stem cells, which divide to both maintain themselves and produce differentiated cells.

options.text: Stem cells disprove the cell theory
options.explanation: Stem cells support cell theory by showing how new cells arise from pre-existing stem cells.
Generally, stem cells produce specialised cells, not the reverse (except in the case of iPSCs).

options.text: There is no connection between stem cells and cell theory
options.explanation: Stem cells directly illustrate the principle that all cells come from pre-existing cells.

toLevel3.question: Stem cells during development create new types of cells, while adult stem cells replace existing types of cells.
toLevel3.explanation: During embryonic development, stem cells differentiate to create the diversity of cell types. In adult life, stem cells replace cells of types that already exist in the body.

toLevel3.question: Self-renewal maintains the {{1}} pool, while differentiation produces new {{2}} cells.
Different tissues have different replacement rates because tissues exposed to more {{1}} need faster {{2}}.
Inner cell mass cells are {{1}} and differentiate into three {{2}} from which all body cell types develop.

toLevel4.question: A person suffers severe burns. Using your knowledge of stem cells, explain how the damaged skin would be repaired.

options.text: Epithelial stem cells at the wound edges divide and differentiate to produce new skin cells
options.explanation: Epithelial stem cells in the surrounding undamaged skin undergo mitosis and differentiation to produce new skin cells that gradually cover the burned area.

options.text: Red blood cells convert into skin cells
options.explanation: Red blood cells cannot convert into skin cells; skin repair requires epithelial stem cells.

options.text: New skin cells form from non-living material
options.explanation: All cells arise from pre-existing cells; skin cells come from stem cell division.

options.text: The body absorbs skin cells from food
options.explanation: Skin cells cannot be obtained from food; they are produced by the body's own stem cells.

toLevel4.question: A patient has low red blood cell counts. Which stem cells would be responsible for correcting this, and where are they located?

options.text: Haematopoietic stem cells in the bone marrow
options.explanation: Haematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow are responsible for producing all blood cells including red blood cells.

options.text: Epithelial stem cells in the skin
options.explanation: Epithelial stem cells produce skin cells, not blood cells.

options.text: Neural stem cells in the brain
options.explanation: Neural stem cells produce nerve cells, not blood cells.
While the lungs contain some stem cells, blood cell production occurs in the bone marrow.

toLevel4.question: Compare the stem cell activity in a growing child versus a healthy adult. How would they differ?

options.text: The child has higher stem cell activity for both growth and development, while the adult mainly uses stem cells for repair
options.explanation: Children need stem cells for growth (increasing body size) and continued development, while adults primarily use stem cells for ongoing tissue repair and maintenance.

options.text: Both have identical stem cell activity
options.explanation: Growing children require significantly more stem cell activity than adults who are primarily maintaining existing tissues.

options.text: Adults have more stem cell activity than children
options.explanation: Children need more stem cell activity to support rapid growth and development.
Both children and adults rely on stem cells, though the balance between growth and repair differs.

toLevel4.question: If a person's epithelial stem cells stopped functioning, predict the consequences for their skin.

options.text: Skin would not be replaced as it is shed, leading to thinning and vulnerability to infection
options.explanation: Without functional epithelial stem cells, the normal 2-4 week replacement cycle would stop, and the skin barrier would deteriorate.
Without stem cells producing new cells, the skin would thin, not thicken.

options.text: Nothing would change because skin does not need replacing
options.explanation: Skin cells are constantly shed and need replacement by stem cells.
The primary consequence would be structural deterioration, not colour change.

toLevel4.question: A developing embryo is at the inner cell mass stage. Predict what will happen next in terms of stem cell differentiation.

options.text: The pluripotent cells will differentiate into three germ layers, each producing specific tissue types
options.explanation: Inner cell mass cells differentiate into ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm, which then produce all the specialised cell types of the body.

options.text: The cells will stop dividing permanently
options.explanation: Cell division continues throughout development; the inner cell mass cells differentiate into more specialised cell types.

options.text: The cells will revert to a zygote state
options.explanation: Normal development proceeds forward, not backward, through the differentiation stages.

options.text: All cells will become blood cells
options.explanation: Only one lineage of cells will become blood cells; the inner cell mass produces all cell types.

toLevel4.question: A bone marrow transplant patient receives healthy haematopoietic stem cells. Describe what these stem cells will do.

options.text: They will self-renew and differentiate to produce all types of blood cells on an ongoing basis
options.explanation: The transplanted haematopoietic stem cells will establish themselves in the bone marrow, self-renewing to maintain the stem cell pool while differentiating to produce red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

options.text: They will only produce red blood cells once
options.explanation: Haematopoietic stem cells produce multiple blood cell types continuously, not just once.
Haematopoietic stem cells are multipotent for blood cells; they do not become skin cells.

options.text: They will stop functioning after transplant
options.explanation: If the transplant is successful, the stem cells will establish and function long-term.

toLevel4.question: An athlete injures their muscle tissue. Explain the role of stem cells in recovery.

options.text: Muscle stem cells (satellite cells) activate, divide and differentiate to repair the damaged muscle fibres
options.explanation: Satellite cells are adult stem cells found in muscle tissue that activate upon injury to produce new muscle cells for repair.

options.text: Embryonic stem cells are released from bone marrow to fix the muscle
options.explanation: Embryonic stem cells are not found in adults; adult muscle stem cells (satellite cells) handle repair.

options.text: The muscle cannot be repaired because muscle cells do not divide
options.explanation: While mature muscle cells have limited division, satellite cells (muscle stem cells) can activate for repair.

options.text: Blood cells convert into muscle cells
options.explanation: Blood cells do not convert into muscle cells; muscle repair relies on muscle-specific stem cells.

toLevel4.question: Without functional epithelial stem cells, skin would {{1}} as shed cells are not {{2}}.
Transplanted haematopoietic stem cells {{1}} to maintain their population and {{2}} to produce blood cells.
Growing children have {{1}} stem cell activity than adults because they need cells for both {{2}} and repair.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why the body maintains separate populations of stem cells in different tissues rather than one central population.

options.text: Because each tissue has unique cell types and repair needs, requiring locally adapted stem cells
options.explanation: Different tissues need specific cell types. Having local stem cell populations ensures rapid, appropriate replacement without needing to recruit and redirect cells from distant locations.

options.text: Because the body cannot transport stem cells
options.explanation: Some stem cells can be transported through blood, but local populations are more efficient for tissue-specific needs.

options.text: Because all stem cells are identical
options.explanation: Different tissue stem cells have different potencies and produce different cell types.

options.text: Because having one central population would be easier
options.explanation: While centralisation seems simpler, local populations provide faster, more specific responses to tissue damage.

toLevel5.question: Compare the consequences of stem cell failure during embryonic development versus in adult tissue.

options.text: Embryonic failure would prevent proper organ formation; adult failure would cause tissue degeneration and loss of function
options.explanation: During development, stem cell failure means essential organs may not form correctly. In adults, failure means damaged tissues cannot be repaired, leading to progressive deterioration.
The consequences differ because the roles of stem cells differ between development (building) and adult life (maintaining).
Adult stem cell failure has serious consequences including tissue degeneration and disease.
Both have serious consequences for organism health and survival.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate the importance of the balance between stem cell self-renewal and differentiation for tissue health.

options.text: Too much self-renewal could lead to tumour formation; too much differentiation could deplete the stem cell pool and stop tissue renewal
options.explanation: The balance is critical: excessive self-renewal resembles cancer (uncontrolled growth), while excessive differentiation uses up stem cells, leaving no source for future replacement.

options.text: The balance does not matter because both processes are beneficial
options.explanation: While both processes are needed, an imbalance in either direction causes serious problems.

options.text: Only self-renewal matters for tissue health
options.explanation: Both self-renewal and differentiation are essential; without differentiation, no functional cells are produced.

options.text: Only differentiation matters for tissue health
options.explanation: Without self-renewal, the stem cell pool would be depleted and tissue renewal would eventually stop.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why the loss of stem cell function is associated with ageing.

options.text: Because declining stem cell activity means tissues are repaired less effectively, leading to age-related deterioration
options.explanation: As organisms age, stem cell populations decrease and become less active, resulting in slower tissue repair, reduced immune function and general decline.

options.text: Because ageing destroys all stem cells instantly
options.explanation: Stem cell decline is gradual, not instant; it occurs over many years.

options.text: Because stem cells are only active during childhood
options.explanation: Stem cells remain active throughout life but their activity gradually decreases with age.

options.text: Because ageing has no connection to stem cells
options.explanation: Declining stem cell function is a significant contributor to age-related tissue deterioration.

toLevel5.question: Compare the stem cell-mediated repair of skin tissue versus a potential future treatment for spinal cord injury.

options.text: Skin repair uses existing adult stem cells naturally, while spinal cord repair would require introducing external stem cells because neurons lack their own
options.explanation: Skin has resident epithelial stem cells for natural repair. Neurons in the spinal cord permanently exit the cell cycle, so repair would require introducing stem cells from an external source.

options.text: Both use the same type of stem cell
options.explanation: Skin repair uses epithelial stem cells; spinal cord repair would require neural stem cells or pluripotent cells.

options.text: Neither can be repaired using stem cells
options.explanation: Skin is routinely repaired by stem cells; spinal cord repair using stem cells is an active area of research.

options.text: Spinal cord repair is easier than skin repair
options.explanation: Spinal cord repair is far more challenging because neurons lack resident stem cells for natural repair.

toLevel5.question: Analyse how the dual role of stem cells (development and repair) connects to the concept of the cell cycle.

options.text: Stem cells must continuously cycle between division and differentiation, using the cell cycle machinery for both growth and tissue maintenance
options.explanation: The cell cycle is the mechanism by which stem cells divide. During development, this produces new cell types; in adults, it replaces lost cells. Both rely on proper cell cycle function.

options.text: Stem cells do not use the cell cycle
options.explanation: Stem cells absolutely use the cell cycle; it is essential for both self-renewal and differentiation.

options.text: The cell cycle only operates during development
options.explanation: The cell cycle continues throughout life in stem cells and other dividing cell types.

options.text: Development and repair use different cellular mechanisms
options.explanation: Both rely on the same fundamental cell cycle machinery for cell division.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate why some tissues heal quickly while others heal slowly or not at all, in the context of stem cell biology.

options.text: Healing speed depends on the availability and activity of local stem cells; tissues without active stem cells cannot self-repair
options.explanation: Skin and blood heal quickly because they have active stem cell populations. Neural tissue heals slowly or not at all because neurons lack active stem cells for replacement.

options.text: All tissues heal at the same rate
options.explanation: Healing rates vary enormously based on stem cell availability and activity.

options.text: Healing speed depends only on blood supply
options.explanation: While blood supply matters, stem cell availability is the primary determinant of repair capacity.

options.text: Tissues that heal slowly simply have too many stem cells
options.explanation: Slow healing is associated with fewer or inactive stem cells, not too many.

toLevel5.question: Analyse why understanding the role of stem cells in development and repair has significant implications for regenerative medicine.

options.text: It suggests that if we can harness stem cell capabilities, we could potentially repair currently untreatable tissue damage
options.explanation: Knowing that stem cells build and repair the body naturally suggests that we could use them therapeutically to treat conditions where natural repair fails, such as spinal cord injuries or organ failure.

options.text: It has no implications for medicine
options.explanation: Understanding stem cell roles is the foundation of regenerative medicine.

options.text: It only applies to understanding embryonic development
options.explanation: The implications extend to adult medicine, particularly for treating degenerative conditions and injuries.

options.text: It proves that all diseases are caused by stem cell failure
options.explanation: While some conditions involve stem cell dysfunction, not all diseases are caused by stem cell failure.
